name: Lavrio
title: Lavrio Ferry & Ship UTM | Thickness Gauging in East Attica
description: Thickness gauging at Lavrio for island ferries, ro-pax ships, coasters and yachts: car deck, ballast tank and hull UTM during winter lay-up or overnight stays.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging for Ferries and Ships Calling at Lavrio
intro: Lavrio, on the south-east tip of Attica, is the island-ferry port for Kea and Kythnos and a departure point for longer routes to the western Cyclades and the north Aegean. Its traffic is passenger and vehicle ferries, with yachts and small cargo ships alongside, and the inspection work they need follows the season: winter lay-up, refits and pre-season checks before the summer timetable. We send technicians from India for each Lavrio job, joining the ship alongside, in its winter berth or at anchor off the port.

highlights.p: Island ferries on the Kea and Kythnos crossings and the longer Cyclades and north Aegean lines run thinner winter timetables. Gauging car decks, ballast tanks and voids fits that quiet period, before the vessels go to dock or return to full service in spring.

highlights.h: Within easy reach of the airport
highlights.p: Lavrio lies a short drive south-east of Athens International Airport, so a team arriving from India gets to a ferry here without long transfers. Short jobs on a laid-up ship or a vessel at a lay-by berth are practical even when the window is only a day or two.

Greek ferry operators buy, sell and redeploy tonnage between seasons. A buyer looking at a ferry lying in Lavrio, or an operator moving a ship to a new route, can have hull, deck and tank readings taken before the decision becomes final.

port.h: Lavrio: an island-ferry harbour in the lee of Makronisos
p: Lavrio lies on the eastern coast of Attica near Cape Sounion, in a bay sheltered on its seaward side by the long, uninhabited island of Makronisos. The channel between the Attica coast, Makronisos and Kea carries ships moving between the Saronic Gulf and the Aegean, so deep-sea traffic passes within sight of the port even though little of it stops. The town grew around the ancient silver mines of Laurion and later around mineral processing, and the old industrial waterfront still shapes the harbour. Today the Lavrio Port Authority runs a compact commercial port given over mainly to passenger and vehicle ferries, beside a large yacht marina and a smaller fishing harbour. Ferries reach the quays through the strait between Makronisos and the mainland, so the final approach is made in sheltered water.

Ferries are the core of the port. Short crossings run to Kea and Kythnos, with more departures in summer, and longer routes connect Lavrio with Syros, Paros, Naxos, Milos and the smaller western Cyclades, and northward with Agios Efstratios, Limnos, Chios and Kavala. The ships on these services range from conventional ro-pax ferries to smaller day ferries on the Kea run, and like much of the Greek coastal fleet, many were bought second-hand from northern European or Japanese owners. Freight lorries for the islands travel on the same ships, so vehicle decks take heavy axle loads as well as cars. Yachts, sailing charter boats and the occasional small cargo or passenger vessel make up the rest of the harbour's traffic, which stays modest compared with the big Attica ports.

The year at Lavrio has two halves. From late spring to early autumn the timetable is full, ferries turn around quickly, and nobody wants a ship out of service. In July and August the meltemi, the strong summer northerly of the Aegean, can make the Kea channel rough and now and then halts small-ferry sailings. From late autumn the island schedules thin out, some ferries leave the route for dry-docking at the Attica yards or at Syros, and others lie in the harbour or at anchor in the bay between voyages or while awaiting employment. That winter stretch is when gauging is easiest to fit in. Tides are negligible, and the shelter given by Makronisos means boarding a ship alongside or at the nearby anchorage is rarely difficult outside winter gales.

facilities.h: Gauging a ship at Lavrio without a drydock
p: Lavrio has no merchant drydock or large repair yard, so the gauging done here is afloat work: on a ferry at its berth between sailings, on a ship laid up in the harbour or the bay over winter, or on a vessel stopping for a few days for repairs carried out alongside by mobile contractors. Afloat, a ro-pax ferry gives access to its vehicle decks, ramps and their hinges, the side shell from inside, ballast and fuel tank boundaries, and voids, provided the tanks can be emptied and certified safe. Bottom plating, sea chests and the underwater hull wait for a docking, and the readings taken here are arranged so they slot straight into that later survey.

When a Lavrio ferry does dock, it usually goes to Perama, Salamina or the Elefsina bay, all within a short passage, or to the Neorion yard at Syros, which serves much of the Cyclades fleet. Readings taken in Lavrio before the ship sails let the operator send a steel estimate with the docking enquiry and compare yards on the same basis. For small craft such as day ferries, workboats and yachts, hull work is often done wherever they are hauled out, and gauging can simply be added to that programme. Ships at anchor off the port are boarded by launch arranged through the agent, which works well in the shelter of the bay.

context.h: Passenger ship rules and the ferry trade from Lavrio
p: Lavrio falls under the Paris MoU, and port state control and harbour supervision are the responsibility of the Hellenic Coast Guard. Most ships calling are Greek-flagged ferries on domestic routes, so their structure is checked mainly through flag and class surveys under the EU rules for passenger ships on domestic voyages, with the Coast Guard inspecting them in port. Ro-pax ships carry features that cargo ships lack: long open vehicle decks, shell doors and ramps, and openings whose integrity matters for stability. Corrosion of vehicle-deck plating and its stiffeners, often hidden under paint and tyre wear, and of ramp hinges and their foundations, therefore gets close attention at every survey.

The commercial side drives the timing. Greek coastal shipping is seasonal, and operators plan dockings, refits and route changes for the winter months, when an idle ferry earns nothing and every survey item has to be closed before the timetable restarts in spring. Many ferries in Greek service were bought second-hand and have traded for a long time, so their ballast tanks, voids and vehicle decks have aged well past the original coating life. An operator who measures those areas in Lavrio over the winter, rather than discovering the scope in dock, can agree steel renewal with the yard in advance and keep the docking short. The same data supports a sale or a charter to another operator.

jobs.h: What ferry operators and owners ask us to gauge at Lavrio
jobs.p: Most Lavrio work comes from ferry operators planning their winter. The usual request is a measured picture of the areas that drive steel renewal on an ageing ro-pax ship, taken while it lies idle so the docking yard receives a firm scope. Buyers and charterers bring a second group of jobs, wanting condition readings on a ferry before a sale or a route change. Merchant ships stopping off the port are less common, but launch-borne work is possible when the agent can arrange access. We set the scope with the operator's technical department, agree with the crew which tanks and voids can be opened, and pass readings back area by area. Typical jobs include:

logistics: Athens International Airport is the arrival point, and Lavrio is reached from there by road through the Mesogeia plain. Entry to the commercial port is under ISPS control, so the ship's agent or the ferry operator arranges passes in advance with the technicians' details and equipment list; launches for ships at anchor are booked the same way. Each technician travels on a Schengen visa obtained in India. For winter lay-up work, the most practical approach is to confirm dates when the operator fixes its docking plan, which leaves time for the visas.

faqs.q: Can a ferry be gauged at Lavrio between sailings in summer?
faqs.a: Only a narrow scope. In summer a ferry's time at the berth is short and every sailing is full, so there is rarely time to empty and certify tanks. Deck plating, ramps and accessible voids can sometimes be measured during an overnight stay. For anything broader, we recommend the winter timetable gap or a lay-up period, when the crew can open tanks in sequence without pressure from the schedule.

faqs.q: Lavrio has no drydock. Is gauging afloat still useful?
faqs.a: Yes, for planning. Most of the structure that decides steel renewal on a ferry, such as vehicle decks, ballast tanks, voids and internal framing, can be measured afloat. Readings taken here give the operator a firm steel estimate to send to the docking yard, so the dock period starts with a known scope. Bottom plating and sea chests are then measured once the ship is dry.

faqs.q: Does the meltemi affect inspection work at Lavrio?
faqs.a: It can affect anchorage work. The summer northerly can make launch transfers in the more open parts of the bay uncomfortable or unsafe, and it sometimes disrupts sailings on the Kea route. Work alongside in the harbour is rarely affected. For jobs on ships at anchor in July and August, we leave a margin in the plan and agree with the agent which days are best for boarding.

faqs.q: Can you check a ferry for a buyer before it changes hands?
faqs.a: Yes. Pre-purchase gauging of a ferry concentrates on the areas that most often need renewal: vehicle-deck plating and stiffeners, ramps and their hinges, ballast and fuel tank boundaries, voids and the shell from inside. The seller's crew prepares the spaces, the buyer's superintendent can attend, and readings are reported against original thicknesses so both sides read the same picture.
